newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US Oct payrolls gain seen easily absorbed.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US Oct payrolls gain seen easily absorbed.

text.p: U.S. credit markets are riding too high to let even a worst-case-scenario U.S. October payrolls report completely dampen the furor, analysts said on Wednesday.

"Even if the numbers on Friday are bearish -- assume the worst -- I still don't think the market will give up most of the gains it made on Tuesday," said Don Fine, chief markets analyst at Chase Asset Management.

The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury soared 1-31/32 to close at 100-27/32 on Tuesday. The rally spilled over to Wednesday's session after fresh data showed U.S. economic growth slowed markedly in the third quarter.
The long bond rose 9/32 to 101-4/32 in early trade before falling 4/32 later in the morning.

Markets are braced for a significant rebound to an increase of 212,000 payrolls in October following September's surprise fall of 40,000 payrolls, a Reuters poll showed. But forecasts ranged wildly from an increase of 145,000 to 350,000 in October payrolls.
The employment report, called by some the world's most watched economic indicator, is set for release by the Labor Department at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Friday, November 1.

Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets, said market players will look behind the headline figure to the underlying components of the report before passing judgment.
"The market is a little reluctant to allow a significant set-back simply because it got an above consensus payroll increase," he said.

The unemployment rate is seen steady at 5.2 percent, while the initial inclusion of the October 1 minimum wage hike to $5.15 per hour should have boosted average hourly earnings one to two tenths to a 0.4 percent gain, analysts said.
However, this forecast remains below September's 0.5 percent increase. The October average workweek is seen increasing to 35.9 hours from 34.7 hours in September.
Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said the market's past hyper-sensitivity to payrolls has been somewhat diminished.
"The market has brought in new players and recontoured the psychology a little bit in terms of inflation and economic performance," Platt said.

"Other numbers (than payrolls) are giving a more constructive backdrop whereas before they were either inconclusive or they themselves were strong and we were hoping the unemployment number would tell us it wasn't so," he added.

While most analysts thought the data powerless to spur a change in short-term interest rate policy by the Federal Reserve before its November 13 confab, a significant rise in the unemployment rate to at least 5.5 percent could persuade the Fed to drop its tightening bias for a neutral stance.
"There is room for (a neutral Fed stance), but they would need to see an unemployment rate of at least 5.5 percent," said David Orr, chief economist at First Union Corp.

Economists said Tuesday's Employment Cost Index's (ECI) relatively weak reading should diminish any lingering Fed inflation worries and give the central bank more room to unwind its presumed bias to tighten interest rates.
"If unemployment jumps to 5.5 percent after this ECI, the Fed may just adopt a neutral stance as opposed to a bias to tighten," Chase Asset Management's Fine said.
Tuesday's ECI rose only 0.6 percent in October following a 0.8 percent gain in September.
Some traders said if payrolls meet expectations, they will use the occasion to reposition more defensively ahead of next week's quarterly refunding by the U.S. Treasury.
